migration_case_study.title: Moving a live commerce platform between two databases without a maintenance window
migration_case_study.context: B2B commerce platform selling annual seat-based contracts; six product lines, each with its own pricing shape; a dozen services; a ~15-year-old MySQL estate replaced by domain services on PostgreSQL, both live with customers throughout. Legacy products were not retired, so the result was two systems of record, both live, converging slowly.
options_rejected: Freeze, dump, restore: unbounded failure mode, no quick way back from a failed restore
Big-bang cutover behind a flag: concentrates all risk in one moment; partial cutovers have no real recovery
Strangler at the edge only: legacy products still read shared identity and subscription records the same day
Application-layer dual-write alone: not one transaction across two engines; correctness that depends on discipline is not correctness
design: Two flows kept strictly separate, with separate code, schedules and failure modes
Flow one: one-time historical backfill, legacy to new, from a read-only snapshot, bounded by a stated historical cut-off, designed to be re-runnable
Flow two: continuous reverse sync, new to legacy, so legacy products keep reading; the new system is the system of record and legacy is a projection of it

Schema: ~30 product-partitioned legacy tables became four generic ones (order, line item, item detail, configuration); product identity moved from table names into columns and a JSON configuration with its own derivation spec
Ordering enforced by the runner: organisations before orders, orders before users and subscriptions
Idempotency in the data, not the runbook: an order is ported only when its external-origin identifier is null, so CRM-originated records are never duplicated

numbers.timeline: Under six months from first specification to steady state
numbers.records_backfilled: consolidated from two upstream systems of record; the exact volume is company data, shared in conversation rather than in public
numbers.specification: ~25,000 words across seven documents; designed and specified by me, executed by a platform team

migration_case_study.lesson: In any dual-write system drift is not a risk, it is a certainty with an unknown arrival time. Reconciliation must exist before the first write; it is part of the mechanism, not a phase after it.
would_do_differently: Write the configuration derivation before the transfer mechanism
Decide and state the historical cut-off on page one
Separate the two flows explicitly, sooner
principles: Separate the one-time historical port from continuous sync
Treat reconciliation as part of the mechanism

modernisation_case_study.title: Replacing a live PHP application with Node.js microservices and Angular, without users noticing
modernisation_case_study.role: Designed and led it, as Lead Software Engineer (2020-2024), with a team of 2 developers. A separate project from the later MySQL-to-PostgreSQL commerce migration.

numbers.duration: 3 months from start to the legacy PHP application being retired

modernisation_case_study.context: The school-facing application ran on PHP with MySQL, with login and sessions in PHP. It had to move to a microservice architecture on Node.js and PostgreSQL with an Angular front end, and the PHP application had to be retired, without schools noticing.
modernisation_case_study.why_not_a_one_time_database_migration: The MySQL database this application writes to is the centre of every product sold to schools. Moving its data off MySQL in one go would have forced every other product to migrate at the same time, which was not possible. So the design supported both databases and both applications at once: the application moved platform by platform while MySQL stayed complete and current for everything else.
approach: APIs first: microservice APIs on Node.js and PostgreSQL were built for all 12 modules up front, and the live PHP application called them after every event, so PostgreSQL stayed current from day one while users kept using PHP

Per-module MySQL flag: every API has a MySQL data layer behind an enable/disable flag per module. Off while a module still runs in PHP (PHP writes MySQL itself); on once the module moves to Node.js, so the API writes MySQL and every product reading MySQL keeps working. Moving a module meant flipping a flag, not running a data migration

Shared login: login stayed in PHP and MySQL; at login the system also issued a JWT for the migrated application; logout destroyed both the PHP session and the JWT, so users always saw one application and one session
Pages moved to Node.js APIs and Angular one module at a time; the Angular UI deliberately kept the existing look so users noticed nothing, while gaining central updates through shared components
New enhancements went only into Node.js and Angular, never PHP, which kept the migration finite
With all 12 modules moved, the MySQL flag is on for every module and the PHP application was retired; the flags stay on until every product that reads MySQL has moved to PostgreSQL
trade_offs: Writes to two databases from application code rely on every write path being covered, by PHP for modules still in PHP or by the API's MySQL layer once the flag is on; acceptable because MySQL must stay current anyway while other products depend on it
Coupled logout must tear down both session mechanisms every time
modernisation_case_study.outcome: 70 pages across 12 modules moved from PHP/MySQL to Node.js microservices, PostgreSQL and Angular in 3 months with 2 developers led by me; no user-visible interruption; the legacy PHP application is fully retired, and MySQL stays current through the per-module flags until the remaining products move to PostgreSQL.

patterns_used: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and clients
Retrieval-augmented generation (hybrid lexical + embedding retrieval, reciprocal rank fusion, cited sources)
Bounded agent loops (step caps) and graceful fallbacks
Guardrails: least privilege, read-only defaults, secrets kept out of the model context
agentic_ai.not_yet_in_record: AWS Bedrock, Vertex AI, LangChain/LangGraph, vector databases and LLM evaluation frameworks are at working-familiarity level (see working_familiarity), not production. The closest production-grade work is the hybrid RAG and tool-calling agent in this portfolio, which implements retrieval, rank fusion, a bounded agent loop and a retrieval eval set from first principles.
llm_engineering_practices: Structured output over free text: review findings come back against a JSON schema (category, severity, file, line, explanation, suggested change), validated with Zod and sent to Gemini as a responseSchema, so the UI and the comment-posting step never parse prose.

Provider abstraction: one review interface over Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini and local Ollama models, so a team chooses its own cost, latency and privacy trade-off; keys stay on the user's machine and requests go straight to the provider.
Live model discovery: the Gemini model list is read from the API and filtered to text models instead of hard-coding IDs, because providers retire model IDs often enough that a fixed list rots.

Context budgeting: lockfiles, build output, binaries and snapshots are filtered out of a diff, the rest fills a character budget smallest-file-first, and the omitted files are named in the prompt so the model says its review is partial instead of guessing.

Recall-first prompting with ranking downstream: the reviewer is told to report every issue with a severity rather than self-filter, and a later step ranks and gates them, which separates detection from prioritisation.
Grounding: the portfolio agent's first step is forced to call a retrieval tool, answers are restricted to retrieved passages, and every answer ships with its sources and tool trace.
Bounded loops: a hard cap on model calls and tool calls per question, with the final step forced to answer, so cost and latency have a ceiling.

Graceful degradation: embeddings fail over to BM25, an LLM outage or quota limit falls back to scripted answers, and unknown tools or bad arguments come back to the model as errors instead of crashing the loop.
Secrets never in the model context: API keys read from the OS keychain at launch (MCP servers, database tools), never in config files, shell history, process arguments or transcripts.

Token cost as a design constraint: compress verbose tool output before it enters an agent's context, answer schema and code lookups from offline indexes, and disable idle MCP servers whose tool definitions tax every request.

rag_design.corpus: A structured career profile (JSON) chunked into ~70 self-contained, titled passages, one per role, system, project, skill group, case-study part and quick answer; titles double as the citations shown to visitors.
rag_design.retrieval: Hybrid: BM25 with light stemming and a domain synonym map, plus Gemini gemini-embedding-001 vectors (768-d, normalised, cosine), fused with reciprocal rank fusion (k = 60) so the two scorers need no score calibration.
rag_design.why_no_vector_db: At ~70 chunks, brute-force cosine in memory takes well under a millisecond; document vectors are computed once per isolate and cached in Cloudflare KV for 30 days. The search() interface is the seam where a vector store (Vectorize, pgvector) would plug in beyond ~10k chunks.
rag_design.evaluation: A retrieval eval set of recruiter questions with the chunks that should answer them, scored as hit@1 and hit@5 on BM25 alone (the worst case) by a headless test run that gates every deploy. It caught a real regression: adding a 'working familiarity' section made 'what are you working on now?' match the word 'working', fixed with a synonym for now/currently.
rag_design.next_steps: LLM-as-judge scoring of answer faithfulness against the retrieved passages, and logging low-score retrievals to grow the eval set from real questions.

genai_quick_answers.genai_experience: Hands-on and shipped, not slideware: an unattended MCP-based pull-request review agent running every 30 minutes at work; this portfolio's agent (Gemini function calling over hybrid RAG, cited sources, retrieval evals in CI); a code-review tool over Claude, Gemini and Ollama with schema-validated output; an MCP server for image generation; and claude-toolkit, ten guardrail and token-cost tools for AI coding agents. I also contributed to a real-time voice-agent pipeline on LiveKit with OpenAI and Gemini realtime models.
genai_quick_answers.rag_experience: I built the retrieval behind this page from first principles: titled chunks, BM25 plus Gemini embeddings fused with reciprocal rank fusion, a KV-cached embedding index, BM25 fallback when the embedding API fails, and a hit@1/hit@5 eval set that runs before every deploy. I have not yet run a vector database in production; at this corpus size it would add cost without benefit, and the search() function is where one would plug in.
genai_quick_answers.llm_providers_and_models: Google Gemini (function calling, embeddings, image generation, realtime), Anthropic Claude (SDK in the code-review tool, and Claude Code with MCP servers day to day), OpenAI realtime models (contributed, voice agents), and local models through Ollama (for example qwen2.5-coder) where code must not leave the machine.
genai_quick_answers.hallucination_control: Force retrieval before answering, restrict answers to retrieved text, show sources and the tool trace, keep the system prompt explicit about ownership words (built vs contributed) and skill levels (production vs working familiarity), and test those rules: a test fails the build if a familiarity skill leaks into the production skills list.
genai_quick_answers.llm_cost_control: Cap model and tool calls per request, retrieve ~1-2k tokens of passages instead of stuffing the whole ~7k-token profile into every prompt, cache document embeddings, budget diff size before it reaches a model, compress tool output before it enters an agent's context, and let teams pick a free or local model where quality allows.
genai_quick_answers.evaluation_approach: Retrieval is measured, not eyeballed: an eval set of real recruiter questions scored as hit@1 and hit@5, run headlessly on every build so a regression blocks the deploy. Agent behaviour is tested against a mocked LLM API: forced first tool call, step cap, thought-signature echo, unknown tools, hidden reasoning. Next is LLM-as-judge faithfulness scoring.
genai_quick_answers.mcp_experience: I build and run MCP servers and clients: the unattended PR-review agent calls its tools through MCP; I wrote an image-generation MCP server with stdio and stateless Streamable HTTP transports sharing one tool definition file; and claude-toolkit manages MCP servers safely (reversible enable/disable with config backups) because every idle server's tool definitions cost tokens on every request.
genai_quick_answers.agent_safety_and_guardrails: Least privilege and reversible by default: production databases read-only unless explicitly overridden, secrets used by the agent but never shown to it, dry-run defaults, tools that only read, same-origin checks and per-IP rate limits on public endpoints, and human review of agent output before it changes anything that matters.
genai_quick_answers.why_genai_roles: Most agent projects are missing what I have spent fifteen years doing: idempotency, audit trails, rollback plans, cost budgets and systems finance can trust. Through 2026 I have been building agents with those properties, at work and in the open, and want to do it full time, as an Agentic AI Architect or on an AI platform team.

projects.name: claude-toolkit

tools: claude-toggle: enable/disable MCP servers without losing config; profiles, backups, restore
claude-vault: secrets in the macOS Keychain, used by AI sessions without being seen
db-conn: Postgres and MySQL queries using vault-stored credentials; production read-only unless --write
squeeze: compresses verbose command output before it enters the transcript
cindex: per-project code index for compact path:line search results
dbindex: offline schema index for all vault database connections

design_principles: Secrets used, not seen; never pass a secret as a CLI argument
Reversible changes: stash instead of delete, back up before every change
Safe defaults: dry-run and read-only unless explicitly overridden
Token efficiency: compact output and cheap offline lookups over live queries

projects.name: AI pull request reviewer (Chrome extension)
projects.summary: Reviews Bitbucket PRs against a configurable standard, with a provider abstraction over hosted and local models so a team picks its own cost/latency/privacy trade-off. TypeScript, React, Manifest V3. Providers: Anthropic Claude (SDK, streamed summaries), Google Gemini (free tier, live model discovery) and Ollama (fully local). Full reviews come back as schema-validated JSON (category, severity, file, line, suggested change) and render as findings anchored to diff lines, postable as inline comments. Diffs are noise-filtered and fitted to a context budget smallest-file-first, with omitted files named to the model. Scheduling runs on chrome.alarms because MV3 service workers are killed when idle.

projects.name: Image-generation MCP server (Nano Banana)
projects.summary: A minimal Model Context Protocol server, in Node.js, that gives Claude real image generation through Google's Gemini image model. Two tools: generate_image (text to image) and edit_image (reference image plus prompt, for consistent series and targeted edits). One tool-definition module is shared by two entrypoints: stdio for Claude Code, and stateless Streamable HTTP for claude.ai custom connectors, deployable to Cloud Run with the included Dockerfile. The API key is read from the OS keychain at launch, so it never lands in config, a .env file or process arguments; the model is pinned by an environment variable so a newer model needs no code change.

working_principles: Specification before implementation: write the spec first, then review the code against it
Schema before endpoint: the schema is what you end up living with
Reversible steps over big-bang cutovers: every migration run could be rolled back at any point
Code review is where the real engineering standard gets set, more than in a style guide
leadership_philosophy: Write the specification, then review against it — make the disagreement happen before the code exists, when it is cheap.
Code review is where teaching happens — the main quality surface and the main development surface at once; built an AI reviewer to take the mechanical half off people's plates.
Guiding ten is different from managing one — influence at that width comes from the artefacts you leave behind: specs, schemas, review comments, service boundaries.

In AI, the unattended MCP-based PR-review agent the team relies on every day.
